Section 3

Most to least serious

Drag the behaviours into order — most serious at the top, least serious at the bottom. Be ready to explain your choices!

  • 1Stealing (shoplifting)⠿
  • 2Speeding on the road⠿
  • 3Cheating in an exam⠿
  • 4Lying to a ticket inspector⠿
  • 5Jumping the queue⠿
  • 6Dropping litter⠿

💡 Think about: Is it against the law? Does it hurt other people? Is it just rude, or is it a crime?

Section 4

Two difficult situations

Read both texts, then answer the questions.

Situation A

I have a colleague at work — let's call him "Marco". He always tells our manager that he works really hard and finishes everything on time. But I know the truth: he usually leaves early and spends a lot of time on his phone. Our manager thinks he's great. I feel it's really unfair to the rest of the team who actually work hard. Marco is a nice person outside work, but what he's doing is dishonest.

Situation B

I think my friend "Sofia" is stealing from shops. I often see her wearing expensive new clothes, but I know she doesn't earn much money. Last week I saw her come out of a clothes shop looking really nervous. She had a new jacket that still had the security tag on it. I know it's against the law, and I'm worried she's going to get into serious trouble. But she's my best friend and I don't want to lose her friendship.

📖 Comprehension questions

1. Why does the person feel it's unfair in Situation A?

2. What makes the person suspicious about Sofia?

3. Which situation do you think is more serious?

Section 5

Structures for giving advice

Study the three levels of advice, then test yourself!

STRONG ADVICE
should / shouldn'tYou should talk to your manager.
You shouldn't ignore it.
ought toYou ought to tell the truth — it's the right thing to do.
MEDIUM ADVICE
If I were you, I'd…If I were you, I'd speak to her privately first.
I think you should…I think you should report it to someone you trust.
GENTLE ADVICE
couldYou could send an anonymous message.
might want toYou might want to wait a little longer before deciding.

Quick quiz — choose the best structure

Your friend is about to use their phone while driving. This is dangerous and illegal. What do you say?

A colleague is upset because they had an argument with their boss. They ask for your advice. What do you say?

Your friend doesn't know what to do about a noisy neighbour. You're not completely sure what the best thing is. What do you say?

Section 6

Complete the conversations

Choose the correct word or phrase. Use the advice structures you've studied.

Dialogue 1

A: My neighbour plays loud music late at night. I can't sleep!

B: Maybe you / / talk to them. Or you / / contact the building manager.

Dialogue 2

A: I haven't finished my report. My boss will be angry!

B: If I / / you, I / / your boss immediately!

Dialogue 3

A: My friend always skips the queue. It's so embarrassing!

B: Tell her she / / do that — it's really rude!

Dialogue 4

A: Is it OK to lie if telling the truth will hurt someone?

B: I'm not sure. You / / try to be honest, but think about how you say it.

Dialogue 5

A: I just need to check one message — I'll drive at the same time.

B: You / / stop the car first. / / , I'd pull over right now.

Dialogue 6

A: What can I do about my noisy upstairs neighbour?

B: You / / talk to them, but they might get angry… You / / contact the landlord instead.

Dialogue 7

A: He used AI to write his whole university essay. I'm annoyed.

B: I'd tell his professor, if I / / you. He / / get away with cheating.

Section 7

Give your advice

Write 2–3 sentences of advice for each situation. Use the grammar structures — the chips light up green when you use them ✓

🎵 Your flatmate plays loud music at midnight every night. You have to get up early for work. What advice would you give them?
should / ought to If I were you, I'd… could / might shouldn't
📱 You found someone's phone on the metro. It's unlocked and you can see their messages. Nobody is around. What should you do?
should / ought to If I were you, I'd… could / might shouldn't
🤥 Your friend asks you to lie to their boss and say they were sick — but they just didn't want to go to work. What do you say to your friend?
should / ought to If I were you, I'd… could / might shouldn't
